title: Throat
description: Oropharyngeal conditions a GDP might encounter or need to refer — from sore throat in the waiting room to an HPV-driven cancer hiding behind a tonsil.

problems.description: A cystic neck lump in a non-smoker, painless and slowly growing, with no obvious ulcer or mass visible in the mouth.
problems.etiology:
High-risk human papillomavirus — almost always type 16 or 18 — is the principal driver [1]. The virus infects the reticulated crypt epithelium of the tonsillar and base-of-tongue tonsils, where it deregulates the cell cycle and drives malignant transformation [2]. HPV-OPC is epidemiologically separate from the tobacco-and-alcohol-driven oral SCC. It is probably sexually transmitted and tends to arise in non-smokers [3].

The reason the neck lump often shows up before the primary is found: the primary tumour is frequently very small — sometimes invisible on imaging — while the nodal metastasis is large, soft, and cystic [4]. That soft, cystic quality in a Level 2 or 3 cervical node in a middle-aged non-smoker should trigger HPV-OPC as the leading differential [4].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically hear:

- A painless lump in the upper neck, noticed incidentally or by a partner.
- Some discomfort on swallowing, as if something is stuck in the throat [5].
- The lump is slowly enlarging over weeks to months [5].

What you'll see:

- A soft, cystic, non-tender cervical swelling, usually at Level 2–3 along the anterior border of sternomastoid [4].
- The mouth and oropharynx can look normal — the primary may be invisible without endoscopy [6].
- **Referred otalgia** is a recognised presentation of oropharyngeal cancer even when the primary is occult [7].
problems.results:
- **Oral and oropharyngeal examination**: normal or shows subtle erythema or asymmetry of the tonsil — but often unremarkable [6].
- **Fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy of the node**: squamous cell morphology with the cystic, lymphocyte-rich pattern typical of HPV-driven disease [8].
- **p16 immunohistochemistry and HPV DNA in-situ hybridisation**: p16 overexpression is the surrogate marker; DNA ISH confirms the virus is present and has deregulated the cell cycle [9]. Both positive together make the diagnosis.
- **PET/CT**: best imaging modality — detects the high metabolic rate of even a very small primary and shows nodal disease simultaneously [10].
- **Endoscopy under GA**: if PET/CT is uninformative, bilateral tonsillectomy and base-of-tongue mucosectomy are performed at the same sitting [11].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that makes HPV-OPC distinct from other head and neck SCCs:

- **Cystic nodal metastasis** — tobacco-driven oral SCC produces firm, hard nodes; HPV-OPC nodes are soft and cystic [4].
- **Non-smoker** — most other oral and oropharyngeal SCCs carry a tobacco history [3].
- **Occult primary** — the primary may be too small to see, yet the metastasis is already large. That reversal of the usual size relationship is the clinical tell [4].
- **Better prognosis than stage-matched HPV-negative disease** [12] — important for counselling.

Distinguish from branchial or lymphoepithelial cysts, which present at the same site and feel similar. Branchial cysts usually present in early adulthood; lymphoepithelial cysts in middle age. But a cystic soft neck lump in any patient over 45 must be biopsied before being labelled benign [8].
problems.treatment:
Refer urgently via the 2-week-wait cancer pathway. A GDP's role is recognition and referral, not treatment.

Definitive treatment at the cancer centre:

- **Radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy** is first-line for most tonsillar, base-of-tongue, and pharyngeal tumours [13].
- **Surgery** (including robotic resection of the primary and selective neck dissection) is offered in some centres as an alternative or adjunct [13].
- **Simultaneous chemoradiation** is particularly effective against poorly differentiated SCCs arising in the tonsil and tongue base [14].

Dental management before radiotherapy is critical: teeth in the planned radiation field with a poor prognosis should be extracted before treatment to reduce the risk of osteoradionecrosis later [15]. Involve the cancer team to plan the timing.
problems.prognosis:
HPV-positive oropharyngeal SCC has a significantly better overall survival than HPV-negative head and neck cancers at the same stage [12]. The improved prognosis is partly explained by increased sensitivity to radiotherapy [12].

For oral and oropharyngeal cancer overall: 5-year survival is ~90% at T1-N0, dropping to ~30% at T2/3-N1 and worse at T4 [16]. The presence or absence of extracapsular spread in cervical nodes is the single strongest prognostic indicator [17].

citations.quote: HPV type 16 and 18 infection is now recognized as an independent risk factor for oropharyngeal SCC. Immunosuppression, e.g. in renal transplant patients or patients with HIV, ↑ the risk of this and other tumours.
There is a very strong likelihood that the primary carcinoma is located in the tonsil or base of tongue because HPV carcinomas start in tonsil crypt epithelium of the major or minor tonsils.

HPV-16 and -18 have become important causes of oropharyngeal cancer. In non-smokers, stage for stage these cancers have a very much better prognosis when treated with conventional techniques. It is probably sexually transmitted (although the exact nature and why most people clear oral HPV infection within a year are not fully understood). It is entirely preventable by vaccination of pre-sexual children with the same vaccine girls are receiving to prevent cervical cancer in most developed countries.

The soft cystic nature of the mass and its site at level 2 or 3 in the neck are highly consistent with metastasis from an HPV associated carcinoma of the oropharynx. This presentation is unlike most other head and neck carcinomas because the primary carcinoma is usually very small, and the metastasis is often large and cystic. HPV associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma also more commonly arise in nonsmokers.
The patient complains of the lump and has noticed some discomfort on swallowing, as if something is stuck in his throat. He assumes the lump is the cause.

If no abnormal tissue is seen on endoscopy, bilateral tonsillectomy and a large mucosal excision (mucosectomy) of the base of tongue are performed because these are the most common sites for HPV associated squamous cell carcinoma. Very occasionally, no primary lesion is found, and the patient is said to have an 'occult primary'. However, even if no primary were found, it would still be almost certain that it lay in the oropharynx, nasopharynx or other head and neck tonsil site because of the presence of HPV. It would simply be that the primary is too small to be found.
Referred otalgia is a common manifestation of pain from the tongue or oropharyngeal cancer.

Metastatic malignancy appears likely, and this lesion is so typical of a cervical lymph node metastasis that it must be considered to be malignant until proven otherwise. The combination of features suggestive of metastasis is the patient's age (should be considered a possible cause in any patient older than 45 years of age), the site (consistent with a cervical lymph node) and lack of tenderness.

Once the squamous cell differentiation is confirmed, current guidelines recommend testing the tissue for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) if no primary is known. This is because HPV and EBV are the causes of many oropharyngeal and most nasopharyngeal carcinomas, respectively. These carcinomas often present with metastasis, and the primary tumour can be very small, so these tests are particularly helpful in directing imaging and further biopsy to either the oropharynx or nasopharynx.

Co-localized positron emission tomography and CT (PET/CT) is the best imaging modality because it shows both anatomical alterations and the high metabolic rate of a cancer, improving the chances of finding even a very small primary carcinoma.

If no abnormal tissue is seen on endoscopy, bilateral tonsillectomy and a large mucosal excision (mucosectomy) of the base of tongue are performed because these are the most common sites for HPV associated squamous cell carcinoma.

Patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma have a significantly better overall survival compared with patients with HPV-negative head and neck cancers. The reasons for improved survival are complex but may be explained, in part, by increased sensitivity to radiotherapy.

Most patients with tonsillar, tongue base and pharyngeal tumours are offered radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as primary treatment. Surgical options, including robotic resection of the primary tumour and neck dissection involving lymph nodes from the deep cervical chain, are also offered in some centres.
Simultaneous chemotherapy and radiotherapy can have a dramatic effect on poorly differentiated SCCs, especially those originating from post-nasal space, tonsil, and tongue base.
Extraction of the second and third molars may often be recommended in cases of tonsillar or tongue base cancer, where a high radiation dose is given to the tooth-bearing area.
90% for T1–N0, but 30% for T2/3–N1 and worse for T4; however, this does not mean that extensive combination therapy and reconstruction is pointless in those with advanced oral cancers.
The presence or absence of extracapsular spread of tumour in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor. Nodal involvement ↓ cure rates by 50%.

problems.description: Sudden severe sore throat with fever, painful swallowing, and inflamed tonsils. Often recurs or follows a run of antibiotics.
problems.etiology: Tonsillitis can be viral or bacterial. The most clinically important bacterial cause is group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — the organism that drives the decision to give penicillin [1]. Viral causes include Epstein-Barr virus (glandular fever), adenovirus, and Coxsackie virus. The reason this matters in a dental context: a patient presenting with sore throat and lymphadenopathy before dental treatment may have glandular fever, and giving amoxicillin or ampicillin to that patient will produce a rash — ranging from mild to anaphylaxis [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically hear:

- Severe sore throat, onset rapid, often with odynophagia (pain on swallowing).
- Fever, general malaise, sometimes headache.
- Voice may be muffled if tonsillar swelling is significant.

What you'll see:

- Inflamed, enlarged tonsils — may show a white or yellow exudate in streptococcal infection.
- Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
- In glandular fever: widespread oral ulceration, petechial haemorrhages at the hard-soft palate junction (pathognomonic when present), and possible hepatosplenomegaly [2].
problems.results:
- **Throat swab**: distinguishes bacterial from viral cause; grows streptococcus and identifies sensitivity.
- **Monospot / Paul-Bunnell test**: screens for EBV in glandular fever. Acute and convalescent titres for CMV and toxoplasmosis if EBV excluded [2].
- **FBC**: raised white count with lymphocytosis in viral infection; neutrophilia in bacterial.
- **Dental relevance**: acute pharyngitis and tonsillitis are contraindications to elective general anaesthesia [1]. Recognise and defer GA-based procedures during acute illness.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing you need to rule out before prescribing: **is this glandular fever?**

Glandular fever mimics streptococcal tonsillitis — fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy — but giving amoxicillin or ampicillin to a patient with glandular fever will trigger a severe rash [1]. The rule: if in doubt, use penicillin rather than amoxicillin for a streptococcal sore throat.

Other distinguishing features of glandular fever:

- Palatal petechiae at the hard-soft palate junction are pathognomonic [2].
- Oral ulceration may resemble primary herpetic gingivostomatitis [2].
- Can be caused by EBV, less commonly CMV or toxoplasmosis [2].
- Early HIV infection can mimic this presentation [2].
problems.treatment:
- **Streptococcal sore throat**: penicillin is the drug of choice [1]. Avoid amoxicillin and ampicillin.
- **Viral tonsillitis / glandular fever**: symptomatic — bed rest, analgesia, soft diet, extra fluids [3]. No antivirals for EBV. Toxoplasmosis may respond to sulfa drugs [2].
- **Recurrent tonsillitis**: refer to ENT for consideration of tonsillectomy. The dental team is not the treating clinician — the role is to recognise, not manage.
- **Dental anaesthesia**: elective GA is contraindicated in the acute phase [1]. Postpone until the patient is well.
problems.prognosis: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis resolves with penicillin. Viral illness — including glandular fever — is self-limiting, typically running 10–14 days for the acute phase [3]. The concern in glandular fever is rare complications: herpetic encephalitis, meningitis, and splenic rupture with contact sport. Recurrent tonsillitis that fails medical management warrants ENT referral for tonsillectomy.

citations.quote: Include the common cold, sinusitis, and pharyngitis/tonsillitis (which may be viral or bacterial), laryngotracheitis, and acute epiglottitis. All are C/I to elective GA in the acute phase. Sinusitis (…… Maxillary sinusitis, p. 422). Penicillin is the drug of choice for a streptococcal sore throat. Avoid amoxicillin and ampicillin, as glandular fever may mimic this condition and these drugs will produce a rash, of varying severity, in such a patient.

This is seen mostly in children and young adults and is spread by infected saliva. It varies widely in severity and presents with sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, headaches, general malaise, and often a maculo-papular rash. There may be hepatosplenomegaly. Oral manifestations may mimic 1° herpetic gingivostomatitis, with widespread oral ulceration, and in addition petechial haemorrhages, especially at the junction of hard and soft palate (pathognomonic), and bruising may be present. The cause is usually Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). Toxoplasmosis can give a similar picture. ∆: initially monospot test, Paul–Bunnell test to exclude EBV, and acute and convalescent titres for CMV and toxoplasmosis. Be aware that early HIV infection can mimic this condition. Rx: symptomatic as for 1° herpes, except toxoplasmosis, which may respond to sulfa drugs; seek expert advice. NB: ampicillin should not be given to patients with a sore throat who may have glandular fever as it inevitably produces an unwanted response, ranging from a rash to anaphylaxis.

It presents with a single episode of widespread stomatitis and unstable mucosa with vesicles which break down to form shallow painful ulcers, enlarged, tender cervical lymph nodes, halitosis, coated tongue, fever, and a general malaise for 10–14 days. Although generally self-limiting, rare complications include herpetic encephalitis and meningitis.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 6014 (self-limiting viral illness — 10–14 days)

problems.description: Intense, paroxysmal shooting pain triggered by swallowing, felt deep in the throat and sometimes radiating to the ear.
problems.etiology: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia follows the same pathophysiological model as trigeminal neuralgia — paroxysmal pain from a sensory nerve — but involves the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) rather than the trigeminal [1]. It is a much rarer condition. The exact mechanism is not stated in the source material. Most cases are idiopathic; compression or demyelination are the postulated mechanisms by analogy with trigeminal neuralgia [2].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically hear:

- Intense, sudden-onset shooting pain deep in the throat, triggered by swallowing — food, saliva, or liquid [1].
- Referred otalgia on the same side [1].
- Pain is paroxysmal — brief attacks, not continuous — and may cause the patient to avoid eating or swallowing.

What you'll see:

- Normal oropharyngeal mucosa between attacks. No visible lesion.
- The diagnosis is largely from history.
problems.results:
- **Topical LA to the ipsilateral tonsillar/pharyngeal region**: immediate relief of symptoms is both diagnostic and therapeutic [1]. This is the key test.
- **MRI brain / skull base**: essential in patients under 50 with cranial nerve neuralgia — must exclude intracranial neoplasm, skull base metastasis, HIV, syphilis, or multiple sclerosis [2].
- **Bilateral neuralgic symptoms**: indicate demyelination until proven otherwise [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The defining feature: **pain triggered by swallowing** and relieved immediately by topical LA to the tonsillar region [1]. That combination separates glossopharyngeal neuralgia from every other cause of throat pain.

Compare to:

- **Trigeminal neuralgia**: same paroxysmal character, but triggered from the face — shaving, cold air, touching a trigger point — not swallowing. Affects the trigeminal distribution, not CN IX.
- **Oropharyngeal SCC**: persistent pain and dysphagia, not paroxysmal; visible or palpable mass usually present eventually.
- **Odynophagia from tonsillitis**: continuous during the infective episode, not paroxysmal, with fever and systemic signs.
problems.treatment:
- **Carbamazepine** is the drug of choice — same as for trigeminal neuralgia [1].
- **Topical LA** to the tonsillar region can break pain cycles [1].
- **Referral**: all patients with cranial nerve neuralgia under 50, and any with bilateral symptoms, need neurological evaluation and MRI [2].
- Refractory cases may need neurosurgical management by analogy with trigeminal neuralgia, but this is outside dental scope.
problems.prognosis: Sources do not give specific outcome data for glossopharyngeal neuralgia. Carbamazepine controls symptoms in most patients with trigeminal neuralgia (80% response rate cited for that condition [3]); by clinical analogy it is the first-line pharmacological option here, but the prognosis data for glossopharyngeal neuralgia specifically are not available in these sources.

citations.quote: This is a similar condition to trigeminal neuralgia but much less common. It affects the glossopharyngeal nerve, causing an intense paroxysmal shooting pain on swallowing. There may be referred otalgia. Topical LA to the ipsilateral tonsillar/pharyngeal region immediately relieves symptoms which may help with the diagnosis. Again, carbamazepine is the drug of choice.

Patients under the age of 50yrs presenting with symptoms of cranial nerve neuralgia require full neurological examination and a MRI scan, as these may be the presenting symptoms of an intracranial neoplasm, skull base metastases, HIV, syphilis, or multiple sclerosis. Bilateral neuralgic symptoms indicate demyelination until proven otherwise.
∆ is by the history, and carbamazepine is useful both therapeutically and diagnostically, with an 80% response rate.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 6331 (trigeminal neuralgia — carbamazepine response rate)

problems.description: Chronic throat and neck pain on swallowing or turning the head, sometimes with pain radiating toward the ear — no visible lesion, no mass.
problems.etiology: An elongated styloid process is the proposed cause [1]. The styloid process normally sits quietly above the attachment of the stylohyoid and stylomandibular ligaments, well clear of adjacent structures. What happens is that when it elongates beyond normal length, it can impinge on adjacent neurovascular structures during jaw movement or head rotation — the internal carotid artery, the glossopharyngeal nerve, or surrounding soft tissue. The reason symptoms vary so widely between patients is that the anatomy differs: the critical variable isn't just length but the angle and direction of elongation relative to the tonsil bed and carotid sheath.
problems.presentation: Dysphagia and pain on chewing are the headline symptoms [1]. Turning the head can reproduce or worsen the pain, which is the distinguishing postural feature. Some patients describe a foreign-body sensation in the throat — as if something is stuck in the tonsillar region — that persists despite normal examination. Referred otalgia is possible. The thing is, many patients will have seen multiple clinicians before landing in a dental or ENT chair because the symptom cluster doesn't fit a clean diagnosis.
problems.results: Examination of the oropharynx is typically unremarkable. Palpation of the tonsillar fossa may reproduce pain — this is useful as a bedside test. Imaging is the key step: an OPG or lateral skull radiograph may reveal the elongated process, but 3D CT of the skull base gives the clearest picture of the process's length and angle. Injection of LA into the tonsillar fossa can provide temporary relief and confirms the anatomical source of symptoms.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of throat pain plus pain on chewing or head rotation — without mucosal lesion — points here, but Eagle syndrome is genuinely rare. The differentials to clear first are glossopharyngeal neuralgia (paroxysmal, touch-triggered on swallowing, immediately relieved by topical LA), oropharyngeal SCC (visible or palpable mass eventually, positive biopsy), and musculoskeletal cervical pain (reproduced by neck movement without throat component). Eagle syndrome sits at the intersection of these: throat symptoms with a postural and movement trigger and a normal-looking mucosa. Confirmed by imaging showing styloid elongation together with symptom provocation on tonsillar fossa palpation.
problems.treatment: Conservative first: analgesia, LA injection into the tonsillar fossa to break pain cycles, and reassurance if symptoms are mild. If symptoms are significant and anatomical confirmation is clear, refer to ENT or oral and maxillofacial surgery for styloidectomy — either trans-oral or external approach. The goal is to shorten or remove the process. Don't operate without imaging confirmation; the diagnosis needs to be solid before any surgical commitment.
problems.prognosis: Styloidectomy relieves symptoms in most patients when the diagnosis has been properly confirmed. Conservative management can manage milder cases long-term. The condition is benign; prognosis is good with appropriate treatment. The main risk is diagnostic delay — patients tend to accumulate investigations and reassurances before the styloid process is imaged.

citations.quote: Dysphagia and pain on chewing and turning the head. It has been proposed that this is due to an elongated styloid process.

problems.description: Unilateral deafness, jaw pain in the lower trigeminal distribution, and restricted mouth opening — with one side of the soft palate not moving — in a patient with no obvious oral cause.
problems.etiology: A malignant tumour invading the lateral wall of the nasopharynx is the mechanism [1]. What happens anatomically is that the nasopharynx sits directly above and behind the soft palate, lateral to the eustachian tube opening. A tumour growing there can simultaneously impair the eustachian tube (causing conductive deafness), compress or infiltrate the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (producing V3 pain and eventually trismus as the lateral pterygoid and masseteric supply is affected), and tether the ipsilateral palate by direct extension or by nerve invasion of the soft palate musculature. The reason this quad of signs is clinically important is that nasopharyngeal carcinoma is often EBV-associated and can grow substantially before becoming visible on routine examination [1].
problems.presentation:
The four cardinal features appearing together on one side:

- Unilateral conductive deafness — often the earliest symptom, dismissed as ear problems [1].
- Pain in the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve: the angle of jaw, lower teeth, lower lip, or chin [1].
- Ipsilateral immobility of the soft palate on phonation or gagging — the affected side doesn't elevate [1].
- Trismus from invasion of the pterygoid muscles [1].

The trismus and palatal immobility are late signs. Early on, patients may present with what sounds like dental pain or ear pain — the nasopharyngeal origin is not obvious.
problems.results: Normal intraoral examination gives false reassurance. The nasopharynx is not directly visible without endoscopy — you need a nasendoscope or rigid pharyngoscope to see the lateral wall. So the sequence is: recognise the symptom quad → urgent ENT referral → nasendoscopy and biopsy. MRI of the skull base is the staging investigation. EBV serology is positive in most nasopharyngeal carcinoma cases. Biopsy of the nasopharyngeal lesion confirms the histology.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The interesting bit is the anatomical logic: four structures on one side all failing simultaneously — ear, jaw nerve, palate, and pterygoid muscles — and all explained by a single mass in the nasopharyngeal lateral wall. No dental pathology produces this combination. TMD produces trismus without deafness or palatal signs. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia produces paroxysmal swallowing pain without motor palatal deficit. A parotid tumour might cause trismus but won't explain the deafness and ipsilateral palatal immobility. The syndrome is essentially pathognomonic when all four signs are present.

A related condition: pterygopalatine fossa syndrome, where the first and second divisions of the trigeminal are affected instead of the third — upper-face pain rather than mandibular pain, same mechanism [1].
problems.treatment: This is outside dental treatment scope. Recognise the symptom combination and refer urgently via the 2-week-wait cancer pathway to ENT or oncology. Don't attempt to treat the trismus or palatal palsy locally — they are signs of malignant invasion, not muscle spasm. Definitive treatment is radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy ± surgery at the cancer centre. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is relatively radiosensitive.
problems.prognosis: Prognosis depends on staging at presentation. The trismus and palatal palsy indicate locally advanced disease (at least T2 by extent). Nasopharyngeal carcinoma has better radiosensitivity than most head and neck cancers, particularly when EBV-associated. However, presentation this late — with skull-base nerve involvement — signals advanced local disease, and prognosis is guarded. Early-stage nasopharyngeal carcinoma detected incidentally carries a much better outcome.

citations.quote: Unilateral deafness, pain in the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, ipsilateral immobility of the palate, and trismus, due to invasion of the lateral wall of the nasopharynx by malignant tumour. Pterygopalatine fossa syndrome is a similar condition where the first and second divisions of the trigeminal are affected.

problems.description: Sore throat or mouth ulcers in a patient with a recent oro-genital sexual history — non-specific in appearance, purulent at the gingival margin.
problems.etiology: Neisseria gonorrhoeae transmitted via oro-genital contact with an infected partner [1]. The reason the oropharynx is involved rather than just the genitourinary tract: the organism is carried in genital secretions and establishes infection on pharyngeal mucosa, particularly in the tonsils and posterior pharynx. Gonorrhoea is 15 times more common than syphilis [1] — it's not a rare organism — but the oral/pharyngeal presentation specifically is uncommon because most infections go unrecognised in the mouth and are attributed to other causes. The Gram-negative intracellular diplococci can survive on mucosal surfaces and produce the characteristic purulent response by triggering an acute inflammatory cascade.
problems.presentation:
Clinically non-specific — that's the problem with this diagnosis:

- Stomatitis or pharyngitis: erythema, soreness, often mild enough to be dismissed [1].
- Superficial ulcers on the oropharyngeal mucosa, persisting despite symptomatic treatment [1].
- Purulent gingivitis: inflamed, bleeding gingival margins with frank pus [1].

So the presentation mimics recurrent aphthous stomatitis, acute herpetic gingivostomatitis, or non-specific pharyngitis. What tips you toward this diagnosis is the persistence — these lesions don't resolve as expected — combined with a history of oro-genital contact. The question is: do you take a sexual history? You need to, or you'll miss it.
problems.results: Swabs from the oropharynx and gingival margin: Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci [1]. Culture confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae and guides antibiotic sensitivity. Urogenital swabs should also be taken — oral gonorrhoea rarely exists in isolation. Testing for co-infection with Chlamydia, syphilis, and HIV is standard when one STI is found.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing that makes this distinct from the other throat and mouth ulcer diagnoses is the combination of persistence, purulent gingivitis, and a relevant sexual history. Acute herpetic gingivostomatitis is more dramatic, resolves within two weeks, and produces vesicular rather than superficial flat ulcers. Aphthous ulcers are recurrent but come in cycles, not continuously, and don't produce purulent gingival inflammation. The purulent gingivitis is not a feature of viral pharyngitis. Gingival involvement alongside pharyngeal ulceration — and the failure to resolve — should prompt the question about sexual history and trigger swabs.
problems.treatment: High-dose penicillin is the traditional treatment [1]. Current UK guidance has shifted toward ceftriaxone IM as first-line given increasing penicillin resistance in N. gonorrhoeae — prescribing should follow current local or national GUM guidelines. Refer to a genitourinary medicine (GUM) specialist [1]: contact tracing is mandatory for a notifiable STI, and the GUM service manages partner notification, co-infection testing, and follow-up swabs. Don't manage this in isolation within the dental setting.
problems.prognosis: Responds well to appropriate antibiotic treatment [1]. Resolution is expected with correct antibiotic therapy and GUM follow-up. The risk if untreated is disseminated gonococcal infection, though this is uncommon from a pharyngeal source. The main clinical risk in practice is missing the diagnosis and treating repeatedly for the wrong condition — persistent oral ulcers not resolving with standard management should trigger this differential.

citations.quote: Gonorrhoea is 15 times more common than syphilis. It results from oro-genital contact with an infected partner and presents as a non-specific stomatitis or pharyngitis with frequent persisting superficial ulcers and purulent gingivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Swabs may reveal Gram –ve intracellular diplococci. Rx is with high-dose penicillin; sexually transmitted infections should be referred to a genitourinary medicine specialist.

problems.description: Severe sore throat with tonsillar exudate and cervical lymphadenopathy in a young person — oral ulceration present, not resolving as expected for tonsillitis.
problems.etiology: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is the cause in most cases; cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a less common alternative [1]. Spread is via infected saliva — it's the 'kissing disease' for a reason [1]. What happens is that EBV infects B lymphocytes via the CD21 receptor in the oropharyngeal lymphoid tissue, driving a massive T-lymphocyte proliferative response that accounts for the lymphadenopathy, tonsillar swelling, and systemic malaise. Most cases occur in children and young adults [1]. The reason it matters clinically beyond its own resolution is the drug interaction: amoxicillin or ampicillin given to a patient with glandular fever will reliably trigger a maculopapular rash — ranging from cosmetically uncomfortable to anaphylaxis [1]. This is why penicillin V, not amoxicillin, is the default antibiotic for sore throats when the cause is uncertain.
problems.presentation:
What you'll see:

- Sore throat, severe — inflamed tonsils with white or grey exudate, resembling streptococcal tonsillitis [1].
- Widespread oral ulceration, similar in appearance to primary herpetic gingivostomatitis [1].
- Petechial haemorrhages at the junction of hard and soft palate — pathognomonic when present [1].
- Generalised lymphadenopathy and fever [1].
- Possible hepatosplenomegaly [1].

The oral ulcers and palatal petechiae are the features that separate glandular fever from a straightforward streptococcal throat in the dental setting. A maculo-papular rash can also appear, especially if amoxicillin has been given already.
problems.results:
- **Monospot test / Paul–Bunnell test**: first-line screening for EBV heterophile antibodies [1].
- **Acute and convalescent titres** for CMV and toxoplasmosis if EBV testing is negative [1].
- **FBC**: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes is characteristic.
- **LFTs**: mildly elevated transaminases in many cases — hepatic involvement is common even without clinical hepatomegaly.
- **Early HIV infection can mimic this presentation exactly** [1] — include HIV in the differential when the clinical picture fits and the monospot is negative.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The palatal petechiae at the hard-soft palate junction are pathognomonic — no other pharyngeal infection produces these reliably [1]. Streptococcal tonsillitis doesn't produce oral ulceration or palatal petechiae. Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis produces vesicles and ulcers but not the tonsillar exudate or the generalised lymphadenopathy pattern of glandular fever. The drug-interaction risk is the most clinically consequential distinguishing feature: amoxicillin given to a patient with glandular fever produces a rash in essentially all cases [1], so any young patient with a sore throat and possible glandular fever should receive penicillin V if antibiotics are needed, never amoxicillin. HIV seroconversion illness is the important mimic — same presentation, negative monospot.
problems.treatment: Symptomatic management: rest, analgesia, soft diet, extra fluids [1]. No antiviral treatment for EBV. Toxoplasmosis, if confirmed, may respond to sulfa drugs — seek GUM or infectious disease advice [1]. Absolutely avoid amoxicillin and ampicillin [1]. If streptococcal co-infection is suspected and antibiotics are indicated, use penicillin V only. Advise the patient to avoid contact sports until confirmed spleen size is normal — splenic rupture is a rare but life-threatening complication.
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting in most cases: the acute phase runs about 10–14 days [2]. Fatigue can persist for weeks to months after the acute illness. Rare complications include herpetic encephalitis, meningitis, and splenic rupture [2]. The takeaway for dental practice: this is primarily a condition to recognise and not inadvertently worsen with the wrong antibiotic. A GDP's role is recognition, safe prescribing (penicillin not amoxicillin), and appropriate referral if complications are suspected.

citations.quote: This is seen mostly in children and young adults and is spread by infected saliva. It varies widely in severity and presents with sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, headaches, general malaise, and often a maculo-papular rash. There may be hepatosplenomegaly. Oral manifestations may mimic 1° herpetic gingivostomatitis, with widespread oral ulceration, and in addition petechial haemorrhages, especially at the junction of hard and soft palate (pathognomonic), and bruising may be present. The cause is usually Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). Toxoplasmosis can give a similar picture. ∆: initially monospot test, Paul–Bunnell test to exclude EBV, and acute and convalescent titres for CMV and toxoplasmosis. Be aware that early HIV infection can mimic this condition. Rx: symptomatic as for 1° herpes, except toxoplasmosis, which may respond to sulfa drugs; seek expert advice. NB: ampicillin should not be given to patients with a sore throat who may have glandular fever as it inevitably produces an unwanted response, ranging from a rash to anaphylaxis.

It presents with a single episode of widespread stomatitis and unstable mucosa with vesicles which break down to form shallow painful ulcers, enlarged, tender cervical lymph nodes, halitosis, coated tongue, fever, and a general malaise for 10–14 days. Although generally self-limiting, rare complications include herpetic encephalitis and meningitis.
